quotes.text: The prompt doesn't create truth. The prompt only steers, which fragments of your tenant co-pilot will consider while it manufactures a response.

quotes.text: Persistent context is not a feature. It's a design decision. It's the choice to stop treating what the model should know as a side effect of whatever happens to be open, recent, or popular in the graph.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Defines the episode's core concept in one clear statement.

quotes.text: A policy statement without control change is not a policy. It's a suggestion that rots. A policy statement without ownership is not a policy. It's a rumor with a URL.

quotes.text: Identity defines who can see. Labels define what can travel. Together they define the context boundary. But again, none of this is a co-pilot feature. It's authorization architecture.

quotes.text: Notebooks don't fix governance. They expose it. They make it obvious when your truth placement is broken. When your source set is stale. And when your permissions model is a disaster.

takeaways: Copilot failures are usually selection and context architecture problems, not prompting problems, because the prompt only steers which tenant fragments get retrieved.
Persistent context means reusable intent plus curated, authoritative sources with owners, lifecycle and review cadence, and Copilot Notebooks are the container that binds them for a defined domain.

Entra permissions and Purview labels, retention and DLP define the real context boundary, so reliable Copilot outcomes require governed identity, traceable outputs and KPIs for quality, cost and control.
hook: Training users to write better prompts will not fix Microsoft 365 Copilot if your tenant has no governed place where intent and truth persist. This episode is for architects, IT leaders and governance teams who want reliable Copilot answers, showing how persistent context, Copilot Notebooks, Entra and Purview turn plausible output into defensible decisions.
